Welcome! This is a playground for **testit**, a tiny testing package for R. It
runs R right in your browser, so there is nothing to install.

Edit this document on the left and click **Run** to see the result on the
right. Break the examples on purpose to see what a failing test looks like, then
fix them again!

# The one rule

If you can write an R expression that returns `TRUE`, you can write a test.

1. Put your checks inside `assert('a message', { ... })`.
2. Wrap every check in **parentheses** `( )`. Each parenthesized expression must
   be `TRUE`.
3. Everything else is ordinary R code (for example, setup).

```{r}
library(testit)

assert('one plus one is two', {
  (1 + 1 == 2)
})
```

No output means all tests passed. Silence is golden.

## Setup code and multiple checks

Lines without parentheses are just evaluated; lines with parentheses are
checked.

```{r}
assert('square root works', {
  x = sqrt(4)  # setup: not checked

  (x == 2)  # checked
  (x > 0)
  (is.numeric(x))
})
```

## When a test fails

The test below fails on purpose. Failed tests report your message and which
check failed.

```{r}
assert('this test fails on purpose', {
  (1 + 1 == 3)
})
```

Try it: edit the check above so that it passes.

# Comparing objects with `%==%`

`a %==% b` is a shortcut for `identical(a, b)`. When it fails, **testit** shows
what is different, which is handy for debugging.

```{r}
assert('identical objects', {
  (c(1, 2, 3) %==% c(1, 2, 3))
  (1:3 %==% 1:3)
})
```

Here `c(1, 2, 3)` is numeric but `1:3` is integer, so they are not identical:

```{r}
assert('numeric is not integer', {
  (c(1, 2, 3) %==% 1:3)
})
```

::: callout-tip
`%==%` binds tighter than `+` and `-`, so wrap the left side in parentheses,
e.g., `((1 + 2) %==% 3)`. Otherwise R reads it as `1 + (2 %==% 3)`.
:::

If numbers only need to be equal up to floating-point error, use `all.equal()`:

```{r}
assert('floating-point numbers', {
  (0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)  # surprise: FALSE
})

assert('use all.equal() for approximate equality', {
  (all.equal(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))
})
```

# Errors, warnings, and messages

Use `has_error()`, `has_warning()`, and `has_message()` to check that code
signals the condition you expect. Optionally, give a pattern to match the text
of the condition.

```{r}
assert('errors are caught', {
  (has_error(log('a')))
  (has_error(stop('oops'), 'oops'))  # also match the error message
  (!has_error(log(1)))               # no error here
})

assert('warnings are caught', {
  (has_warning(warning('watch out')))
  (has_warning(1:2 + 1:3, 'longer object'))
})

assert('messages are caught', {
  (has_message(message('hello')))
  (has_message(message('hello'), 'hel'))
})
```

# Test your own function

A realistic workflow: write a function, then describe its behavior with tests.
Edit `fizzbuzz()` to introduce a bug and see which check complains.

```{r}
fizzbuzz = function(n) {
  if (n %% 15 == 0) return('FizzBuzz')
  if (n %% 3 == 0) return('Fizz')
  if (n %% 5 == 0) return('Buzz')
  as.character(n)
}

assert('fizzbuzz() handles each case', {
  (fizzbuzz(3) %==% 'Fizz')
  (fizzbuzz(5) %==% 'Buzz')
  (fizzbuzz(15) %==% 'FizzBuzz')
  (fizzbuzz(7) %==% '7')
  (has_error(fizzbuzz()))
})
```

Now it's your turn: write an `assert()` for a function of your own below.

```{r}
assert('my first test', {
  (TRUE)
})
```

# Next steps

In a real package, put test files named `test-*.R` in `tests/testit/` and add
`tests/test-all.R`:

```r
library(testit)
test_pkg('yourpkg')
```

Then `R CMD check` runs your tests automatically. **testit** can also check
printed output with Markdown snapshot files (`test-*.md`); see the
[README](https://github.com/yihui/testit#readme) for snapshots, helper files,
and how to convert **testthat** tests.
